vulnerability: Missing validation of _fromJar allows forced strategy withdrawal and donation attack
reason: The function trusts the user-supplied _fromJar address and calls IJar(_fromJar).token(), getRatio(), decimals(), and IStrategy(strategies[_fromJarToken]).withdrawForSwap(...) without verifying that _fromJar is the legitimate jar for _fromJarToken (i.e., jars[_fromJarToken] == _fromJar). An attacker can deploy a malicious contract implementing the IJar interface that returns a legitimate token such as DAI, a controlled getRatio(), and a controlled decimals(). Its transferFrom() can be a no-op. The attacker calls swapExactJarForJar with this malicious _fromJar and a large _fromJarAmount. The Controller computes a large _fromJarUnderlyingAmount and, because the malicious jar has insufficient real underlying, calls the legitimate strategy's withdrawForSwap() for the difference. In typical Yearn-style strategies, withdrawForSwap() withdraws real underlying and transfers it to the legitimate jar registered in jars[want]. This is a donation to the legitimate jar, increasing the underlying value per jar share. The attacker can first acquire a large amount of legitimate jar shares (e.g., via flash loan), trigger this donation, and then redeem the shares for a profit, draining strategy funds from other jar holders. This is a critical theft-of-funds vulnerability.

vulnerability: Missing validation of _toJar allows theft of Controller token balances via approval to malicious jar
reason: The function trusts the user-supplied _toJar address. It derives _toJarToken = IJar(_toJar).token(), then after executing the swap it reads the entire Controller balance _toBal = IERC20(_toJarToken).balanceOf(address(this)), approves _toJar to spend _toBal via safeApprove, and calls IJar(_toJar).deposit(_toBal). There is no check that _toJar is the legitimate jar for _toJarToken (i.e., jars[_toJarToken] == _toJar). An attacker can supply a malicious _toJar contract whose token() returns any ERC20 token held by the Controller. The malicious deposit() function can then call IERC20(_toJarToken).transferFrom(address(this), attacker, _toBal) using the freshly granted allowance, stealing the entire Controller balance of that token. The malicious contract can also return a fake balanceOf() and transfer() so that the later _toJarBal < _toJarMinAmount check passes and the stolen value is reported back to the caller. This allows direct theft of any ERC20 balance held by the Controller, including temporarily held funds during a swap or accidentally stuck tokens. This is a critical direct theft vulnerability.

vulnerability: Strategist can set an arbitrary malicious jar and irreversibly hijack the jar mapping
reason: setJar allows the strategist (a hot role that is not protected by a timelock) to set jars[_token] to any address when no jar is currently set. There is no validation that _jar is a legitimate contract, that IJar(_jar).token() == _token, or that _jar is the intended jar for the token. Once set, the mapping cannot be changed because setJar requires jars[_token] == address(0). A malicious or compromised strategist can set jars[_token] to their own contract before the legitimate jar is registered. The malicious contract can then call Controller.withdraw(_token, amount), which passes the msg.sender == jars[_token] check, causing the legitimate strategy to withdraw funds and send them to the malicious jar (or otherwise allow the attacker to receive the funds). The same mapping also prevents the legitimate jar from calling Controller.withdraw because its address no longer matches jars[_token], freezing user funds. This is a critical centralization/privilege vulnerability that enables theft of all strategy funds for a token with no existing jar.
